items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: So the first year I recorded the George Lewis climax records.

ctx.x: The reason I got into the business at all was partly due to these first records I mentioned, the Jazzmen, that were so badly recorded on the little machine. About a $200 list price machine it was, a federal recorder. Some kid that worked, he was a teenage kid, I guess, that worked for Grunewald's. Happened to have it. He's the only one we could find that had any blanks around that would be able to record the band in 1942 when Dave issued the records. And those records were so bad that I'll tell you one story that…

He hadn't thrown them out fortunately, but he probably would have very soon if Dave hadn't gotten back. He could have thrown them in a wastebasket. So he thought it was just a joke, you know, that he sent something to amuse him. So Dave said, no, that's the real thing. It had to be worked on and issued. So anyway, I decided after that that I couldn't do much worse. So I got a machine. My machine only cost about $40. My brother put a little secondhand machine together and then bought an amplifier. My brother was a…
This is the fourth, okay, I got the fourth reel on.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: Incidentally, even George Lewis used to do it in New York around 1942.

ctx.x: He said, here's a man who knows all my pieces and all. He was very pleased. So after talking a while, he said he'd made so many records he couldn't remember all of them. He mentioned, at that time, we didn't know all of his records either and we still probably don't. But he mentioned he'd made some under other names and all too. But that might have been something like those Vocalions. He didn't have his name on all of those. Anyway, when the subject of Simeon came up and also about Earl Hines, that Simeon was…
I don't know any other pianists in the... Do you?

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: the fellow who had been in Yvonne Thomas' band out west Louisiana at the time Yvonne was killed. It turned out to be George Lewis.

ctx.x: Well, he probably hadn't lived here since 1918, I guess.

Yeah, and probably hadn't heard Big Eye much since those days either. But, um, Bunk seemed to want to use Big Eye. And the, as soon as Bunk got into town that morning we went over to see Big Eye. We, I told him that Big Eye had taken sick the Saturday night before, and had to quit playing in the middle of the job that Saturday night. Uh, Mrs. Lutgen made him sit there on the stand throughout the night, though, to make it look like it was a bigger band. It was only about a three-piece band, maybe four pieces at…

I would have known it all over. This was downtown, all the way down to the Ninth Ward, where his son lives, which was out of his territory, more or less, you'd think, because he was an uptown man. Well, anyway, this is the one of the few times, at least we'll say, that Bunk's memory wasn't quite right. He said there's a clarinet player by the name of Stuart. I thought he said Strode or something at first, but it was just Bunk's heavy accent again. I'm sure he was saying the Stuart. Do you remember what the…
